summary: Describes a language tag for indicating the language used in an information object. It is on the standards track. It has been replaced by RFC 3066 and RFC 3282.

plainLanguage.summary: A short label, such as en or en-US, that says which human language some text, audio or video is in. The RFC defines the shape of that label, a header that carries it, and a way for mail programs to choose between versions of the same message in different languages.

questions: how to identify language of content
subtitle: The original scheme for labelling content with a language, such as en or en-US, plus the Content-Language header.

tldr.problem: People prefer information in a language they understand, but there was no standard way to label content with the language it is written in.
tldr.mechanism: A language tag is a primary tag plus optional subtags, each of 1 to 8 letters, joined by hyphens. Two-letter primary tags follow ISO 639, and the RFC adds a Content-Language header and a differences parameter for multipart/alternative.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was replaced by RFC 3066 and RFC 3282.

facts.label: Reserved primary tags
facts.value: i for IANA registrations, x for private use

today: RFC 1766 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3066 and RFC 3282, so those are the documents to follow instead.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Many languages are spoken by human beings, and a great many of those people would prefer to have information presented in a language that they understand. In some contexts it is possible to have information in more than one language, or to provide tools that help with understanding a language, such as dictionaries. For any of those to work, there must first be a way of labelling the information content with an identifier for the language in which it is written.

In the tradition of solving only problems that the authors think they understand, this document specifies an identifier mechanism, and one possible use for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a mail program or a web page can offer a version of something in your language, something has to record which language each version is in. This RFC defines that label.

sections.title: The Language Tag
sections.content:
A language tag is composed of one or more parts: a primary language tag and a possibly empty series of subtags. The syntax in RFC 822 EBNF is Language-Tag = Primary-tag *( "-" Subtag ), where both the primary tag and each subtag are 1 to 8 letters. Whitespace is not allowed within a tag, and all tags are to be treated as case insensitive; conventions for capitalisation exist but carry no meaning.

The RFC predefines what the parts mean. In the primary tag, all two-letter tags are interpreted according to ISO 639, the value i is reserved for IANA-defined registrations, and the value x is reserved for private use, whose subtags IANA will not register. Other values cannot be assigned except by updating this standard.

In the first subtag, all two-letter codes are ISO 3166 alpha-2 country codes denoting the area in which the language is used, and codes of 3 to 8 letters may be registered with IANA by anyone who feels a need for it. The information in that subtag may be a country identification such as en-US, a dialect or variant such as no-nynorsk or en-cockney, a language missing from ISO 639 that is not a variant of any listed language, registered with the i prefix as in i-cherokee, or a script variation such as az-arabic and az-cyrillic. In the second and subsequent subtag, any value can be registered.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag is a main part and then optional extra parts, joined with dashes. The main part is normally a two-letter language code from ISO 639, and the first extra part is often a two-letter country code from ISO 3166. Capital letters are a convention only and carry no meaning.

sections.title: What a Tag Means
sections.content:
The language tag always defines a language as spoken or written by human beings for communication of information to other human beings. Computer languages are explicitly excluded. There is no guaranteed relationship between languages whose tags start out with the same series of subtags; in particular, they are not guaranteed to be mutually comprehensible, although this will sometimes be the case.

Applications should always treat language tags as a single token. The division into main tag and subtags is an administrative mechanism, not a navigation aid. The relationship between the tag and the information it relates to is defined by the standard describing the context in which it appears.

The RFC gives examples. For a single information object the tag is the set of languages needed for a complete understanding of the object. For an aggregation, such as a document store or a library, it is the set of languages used inside its components. For an object whose purpose is to provide alternatives, it is a hint that the material inside is provided in several languages, and that one has to inspect each alternative to find its language or languages.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag names a human language, never a programming language. Two tags that start the same do not mean the speakers understand each other. A program should treat the whole tag as one value rather than splitting it up.

sections.title: The Content-Language Header
sections.content:
The header is intended for use where one wishes to indicate the language or languages of something that has RFC 822-like headers, such as MIME body parts or web documents. Its grammar is Language-Header = "Content-Language" ":" 1#Language-tag, so it may list several tags separated by commas. Whitespace is allowed, which also means that parenthesised comments can be placed anywhere in the language sequence.

The examples in the RFC show a Norwegian official document with parallel text in both official versions of Norwegian, a voice recording from the London docks tagged en-cockney, a document in Sami, a language with no ISO 639 code that has six mutually incomprehensible dialects, tagged i-sami-no, an English-French dictionary tagged en, fr, an official EC document in several of its official languages, and an excerpt from Star Trek tagged x-klingon. The RFC notes that none of the subtags shown in the document have actually been assigned; they are used for illustration only.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a line at the top of a message that says which language the content is in. It can name more than one language, separated by commas.

sections.title: The Differences Parameter
sections.content:
When the MIME multipart/alternative body part is used, it is possible to have the body parts give the same information content in different languages. In that case a Content-Language header should be put on each body part, and a summary Content-Language header on the multipart/alternative itself.

As defined in RFC 1541, multipart/alternative has only one parameter, boundary, and the common use of the type is to offer the same message in more than one format. Using language tags to tell the alternatives apart will not lead all MIME user agents to present the most sensible body part as default, so the RFC defines a new parameter. Its name is Differences and its value is one or more of Content-Type and Content-Language. Further values can be registered with IANA, and each must be the name of a header for which a definition exists in a published RFC. If the parameter is absent, Differences=Content-Type is assumed.

The intent is that the MIME reader can look at those headers and choose what to present to the user, based on knowledge of the user's preferences and capabilities. The mechanism for deciding which body part to present is outside the scope of the document. When composing a message, non-MIME mail readers will show the first body part first, so that should most likely be the language understood by most of the recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes one message carries the same text in several languages. The new parameter tells mail programs which headers to compare, so the program can show the version in the reader's language.

sections.title: Registration of New Tags
sections.content:
Any language tag must start with an existing tag and extend it. A requester fills in the registration form, giving the name and email address of the requester, the tag to be registered, the English name of the language, the native name transcribed into ASCII, and a reference to a published description of the language, such as a book or an article.

The form must be sent to the IETF types list for a two-week review period before it goes to IANA. When the two weeks have passed, the language tag reviewer, who is appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director, either forwards the request to IANA or rejects it because of significant objections raised on the list. Decisions made by the reviewer may be appealed to the IESG.

The RFC's Security Considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in the memo. On character sets, codes may always be expressed using the US-ASCII character repertoire, and the memo does not address deciding the rendering of a character set from the language tag, because it is thought impossible to make that decision correctly in all cases unless means of switching language in the middle of a text are defined.
sections.plainLanguage: To add a new language label, you fill in a form, the list reviews it for two weeks, and a reviewer then sends it on to IANA or turns it down. Anyone who disagrees with the reviewer can appeal to the IESG.

viz.caption: THE MIME EXAMPLE FROM RFC 1766, SECTION 4.1

data.title: multipart/alternative by language
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/alternative; differences=Content-Language;
          boundary="limit"
Content-Language: en, fr, de

--limit
Content-Language: fr

Le renard brun et agile saute par dessus le chien paresseux
--limit
Content-Language: de
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=iso-8859-1
Content-Transfer-encoding: quoted-printable

Der schnelle braune Fuchs h=FCpft =FCber den faulen Hund
--limit
Content-Language: en

The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog
--limit--
